records.sourceFile: Assessing isometric kicking force and post-match responses using the Kicker test.pdf

paper.citation: Thomas RJ, Timmins RG, Tofari PJ, Williams MD, Opar DA. Assessing isometric kicking force and post-match responses using the Kicker test. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022.
paper.abstract: This study examined the inter-session reliability of a novel isometric Kicker test of combined hip flexion and knee extension force, and whether it could monitor force for 72 h after soccer matches. Reliability was high across sessions, and in academy soccer players Kicker force remained below baseline at 24, 48 and 72 h after matches in both limbs.
paper.tldr: A field-based isometric test of combined hip flexion and knee extension showed good reliability, and force stayed suppressed for 72 h after matches in academy soccer players. The authors propose it as a monitoring tool once athletes are familiarised, but it was not tested against injury or return-to-play outcomes.
paper.methods: Part A: 20 participants (13 male, 7 female; recreational or higher) completed the Kicker in three sessions across consecutive weeks, with the best of three maximal efforts per limb used; reliability was summarised with ICC, typical error, %CV and MDC95. Part B: 17 male academy soccer players were tested at baseline and at +24, +48 and +72 h after matches over three weeks, after a familiarisation week, and analysed with a linear mixed model (player as random intercept) and effect sizes.
paper.findings: Inter-session ICC was 0.91 to 0.98 and %CV was 3.7 to 10.3 (Table 1); typical error fell from 17.6 N to 9.5 N for the preferred limb after initial exposure. After matches, Kicker force was below baseline at every time point in both limbs (preferred -10.7% at +24 h, -12.5% at +48 h, -5.8% at +72 h; non-preferred -9.2%, -9.8%, -7.8%; all p < 0.01), with effect sizes of d -0.26 to -0.43, which the authors' scale rates as small.
paper.limitations: The abstract's post-familiarisation reliability figures (ICC above 0.95, typical error below 14 N, CV below 6%, MDC below 40 N) match the session 2 to 3 rows of Table 1; session 1 to 2 error was larger (typical error about 18 N, CV up to 10.3%, MDC95 49 N). The post-match group was a convenience sample of 17 academy players with no external load data, no testing beyond 72 h, unexplained outliers, and reliability measured in a different, older recreational cohort; the device was supplied free of charge by its manufacturer.
paper.practicalImplications: The Kicker takes under 5 minutes per athlete, and a familiarisation session is needed because error fell after the first session. The authors suggest that after familiarisation, changes beyond the 5.3% CV, or beyond the MDC95 of 26 to 38 N, can be treated as real, and that post-match deviations could guide shooting or sprinting volume for 72 h after a match; this use was not tested.
paper.athleteDev: Use the Kicker after a familiarisation block to track force against an individual baseline, treating changes beyond the MDC95 (26 to 38 N for sessions 2 to 3) as meaningful. The evidence is from healthy recreational and academy soccer players, and does not show that the test predicts injury or sets training thresholds.
paper.rtp: Not validated for return to sport. Only healthy players were tested, so the study cannot set return-to-kicking or return-to-play criteria; the authors suggest a possible future role in kicking progressions after rectus femoris injury, which was not studied.

records.sourceFile: Assessing the Validity of Wearable Inertial Sensors in Evaluating Joint Kinetics and Hamstring Musculotendon Mechanics at Various Running Speeds.pdf

paper.citation: Lin YC, Price K, Carmichael D, Maniar N, Hickey J, Timmins RG, et al. Assessing the Validity of Wearable Inertial Sensors in Evaluating Joint Kinetics and Hamstring Musculotendon Mechanics at Various Running Speeds. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025 (published ahead of print).
paper.abstract: This validation study compared inertial measurement unit (IMU) and optical motion capture (OMC) estimates of sagittal-plane joint moments and hamstring musculotendon mechanics in 18 healthy adults running on a treadmill at 70% to 100% of maximal speed. The authors report close waveform agreement overall, with better agreement for knee than hip moments, and an IMU overestimate of peak hip extension moment at higher speeds.
paper.tldr: Wearable IMUs combined with musculoskeletal modelling reproduced optical-capture knee moments and hamstring strain and velocity waveforms well during treadmill running in healthy adults. Peak hip extension moment was overestimated more as speed rose, and peak hamstring force limits of agreement were wide for BFLH and SM, so the method needs checking before field use.
paper.methods: Eighteen healthy, recreationally active adults ran on an instrumented treadmill at six speeds from 70% to 100% of their maximal speed, with simultaneous Vicon and Xsens data and hamstring EMG. Two participant-specific OpenSim models (one per system) were used for inverse dynamics and muscle force estimation, and agreement was assessed with RMSE, NRMSE, CMC, Bland-Altman analysis and linear mixed models of RMSE against speed. Joint moments and muscle forces were compared over the swing phase only.
paper.findings: Median CMC was above 0.96 for hip and knee moments in swing, and 0.88 to 0.98 for hamstring muscle forces; hamstring strain and velocity CMC were above 0.98 at all speeds. The IMU system overestimated peak hip extension moment, with bias rising from 0.12 Nm/kg at 80% speed to 0.47 Nm/kg at maximal speed, and overestimated peak knee flexion moment by 0.07 to 0.15 Nm/kg. Limits of agreement for peak hamstring force were wider for BFLH and SM (above 0.57 BW) than for BFSH and ST (above 0.16 BW).
paper.limitations: Only one IMU system (Xsens) and one optical system (Vicon) were tested, using the manufacturer's own Kalman filter for IMU joint angles, and separate musculoskeletal models were built for each system. Comparisons were restricted to swing phase on a treadmill, in recreationally active adults with a mean maximal speed of 7.44 m/s. The abstract gives the RMSE increase per 1 m/s for joint moments in N/m, but the results report it in Nm/kg (0.23 for hip, 0.04 for knee); the results values are used here, and the peak hip moment bias is given as 0.47 Nm/kg at maximal speed in the results but 0.49 Nm/kg at 95% speed in the discussion.
paper.practicalImplications: The results support using this IMU approach for knee flexion moment and hamstring strain waveforms during running, where agreement was excellent. Peak hip extension moment bias grew with speed (above 10% of the optical value from 85% speed), and peak lengthening velocity was systematically overestimated for BFLH, SM and ST, so staff should validate these outputs in their own set-up before comparing athletes or setting loading targets.
paper.athleteDev: IMU-based estimates of hamstring strain and knee moment tracked optical capture well across running speeds in healthy adults, which supports their use as a trend measure of sprint mechanics. Peak hip moment and peak BFLH and SM force carry wide limits of agreement (hip up to about 1.5 Nm/kg; BFLH and SM force 0.57 to 1.2 BW), so they should not be used for absolute load comparisons between athletes without local validation.
paper.rtp: Not designed for return to sport. The sample was healthy and recreationally active, with no injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes. The hamstring late-swing focus relates to injury risk, but the study does not test whether these estimates track injury, healing or readiness to return to running.

records.sourceFile: Assessing the cumulative effect of long-term training load on the risk of injury in team sports.pdf

paper.citation: Bache-Mathiesen LK, Andersen TE, Dalen-Lorentsen T, Clarsen B, Fagerland MW. Assessing the cumulative effect of long-term training load on the risk of injury in team sports. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2022;8:e001342.
paper.abstract: This study set out to determine how to assess the cumulative effect of training load on injury or health problem risk in team sports. A simulation based on a football dataset compared seven modelling methods, and the best-performing method, a distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM), was then illustrated on a youth handball cohort.
paper.tldr: In simulated team-sport data, a distributed lag non-linear model recovered cumulative training-load effects more accurately than rolling averages, EWMA, REDI, ACWR or week-to-week change. The handball demonstration found no statistically significant effects, so the method is not yet a basis for load decisions.
paper.methods: Simulated players were given sRPE values sampled from a 36-player Norwegian Premier League football dataset, with 250 players followed for 300 days. Seven time-dependent relationships were simulated for absolute and relative (daily %change) load, and seven methods were compared on RMSE, AIC and 95% CI coverage over 1900 simulations. The DLNM was then fitted to 205 Norwegian elite youth handball players (471 self-reported health problems; 64% of sRPE values missing and imputed) using Cox regression adjusted for sex and age, with a frailty term for recurrent events.
paper.findings: For absolute load, DLNM had the lowest external RMSE in every scenario (1.44 vs 4.77 to 5.53 under the constant scenario; 0.76 vs 1.88 to 2.13 under exponential decay) and the lowest AIC in almost all simulations. EWMA outperformed rolling average under decay scenarios, and no method recovered the direct-then-inverse relationship. In the handball data, high sRPE (above 4000 AU) was associated with a hazard ratio of about 1.2 or more on the current day, with high uncertainty; none of the effects were significant (p >= 0.8).
paper.limitations: The simulated relationships were chosen by the authors, and the simulation assumed day-to-day differences matter, which favoured DLNM for relative load. The handball analysis had poor data quality, few covariates and no causal design, and the authors caution that the effects may be spurious. Only seven methods and a limited set of ACWR variants were compared.
paper.practicalImplications: When analysing cumulative training load and injury or illness in team sports, a distributed lag model can show how load magnitude and time since exposure interact, which rolling averages and single ratios cannot. For absolute load, the authors describe EWMA as a simpler alternative when the aim is to adjust for training load rather than estimate its effect. The handball output should not be read as a load threshold because none of its effects were significant.
paper.athleteDev: For analysts modelling load and injury data, the simulation favours DLNM, and EWMA over rolling averages or REDI, for absolute load; ACWR and week-to-week change failed to detect the simulated relationship in some scenarios. It is a statistical methods comparison, not evidence for specific training load thresholds, and the handball example did not show a significant link between load and health problems.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study models self-reported health problems in team-sport squads and does not use rehabilitation or return-to-play data, so it cannot set return-to-play load criteria.

records.sourceFile: Athlete monitoring perspectives of sports coaches and support staff - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Timmerman WP, Abbiss CR, Lawler NG, Stanley M, Raynor AJ. Athlete monitoring perspectives of sports coaches and support staff: A scoping review. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2024:1-20.
paper.abstract: A scoping review of 42 studies that explored the perspectives of sports coaches and support staff on athlete monitoring. Most studies were from the Anglosphere and involved national or international level teams. Coaches and staff most often monitored to reduce injury and illness, inform training and maintain performance, and they valued monitoring while emphasising communication and the limits of quantification.
paper.tldr: Coaches and support staff generally see athlete monitoring as useful for managing injury, training and performance, but they say no single scientific approach is perfect and that conversation with athletes remains essential. The evidence is largely self-reported perspectives from a narrow set of countries and levels.
paper.methods: Scoping review following the JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR, searching SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE, APA PsycInfo and Embase up to 6 September 2022. Two reviewers screened records and full texts, one author charted data, and frequency analysis was combined with topic summaries of qualitative findings. No formal quality appraisal was done.
paper.findings: Of 4,381 records, 42 studies met the criteria, and 55% (23 of 42) were published since 2020. Training load was the most studied focus (11 of 42 studies). Of the 23 studies reporting purposes, the most common were reducing injury and illness (12), informing training (8) and improving or maintaining performance (8). Expected effectiveness was significantly higher than perceived effectiveness in one football study (Akenhead and Nassis, 2016), and sex or gender was reported in only 18 of 42 studies, with women averaging 16% of samples.
paper.limitations: Most studies were in English-speaking countries and at national or international level, and few reported participant characteristics clearly. Terms such as elite were not defined, and the review did not separate perspectives by role or athlete level. The search omitted some terms (for example medical staff and assess or evaluate), and data were charted by one reviewer.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who plan monitoring should expect coaches and support staff to value subjective information and regular conversation with athletes alongside objective data, and to cite time, expertise, resources and buy-in as the main barriers. Where expected and perceived effectiveness were compared (football staff, and gymnastics coaches and medical staff), perceived effectiveness of training load monitoring was lower than expected, which supports checking how monitoring data are actually used rather than assuming value.
paper.athleteDev: Coaches in the included studies reported using athlete self-report measures as a conversation starter and early alert, and combining load data with athlete feedback and coach observation when adjusting training. The review describes these practices but does not test whether any monitoring approach improves performance.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It summarises coach and staff perceptions of monitoring and does not report injured athletes, return timelines or return outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Awareness and Perceived Value of Eye Tracking Technology for Concussion Assessment among Sports Medicine Clinicians A Multinational Study.pdf

paper.citation: Snegireva, N., Derman, W., Patricios, J., Welman, K.E. Awareness and Perceived Value of Eye Tracking Technology for Concussion Assessment among Sports Medicine Clinicians: A Multinational Study. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2020;48(2):165-172.
paper.abstract: Cross-sectional online survey of 171 sports medicine clinicians from 32 countries on their awareness and use of eye tracking for concussion assessment and their views on its value. Few clinicians had used eye tracking, most relied on their own clinical assessment, and about half saw potential benefit in the technology. The authors call for more education and practical experience with concussion assessment tools.
paper.tldr: Few sports medicine clinicians had used eye tracking for concussion, and most relied on standard clinical assessment. About half saw potential benefit, mainly for its objectivity and ease of use.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional online survey (18 questions, Google Forms) distributed by email to sports medicine associations and through LinkedIn, Twitter and conference channels from January to December 2017. Responses came from 171 clinicians in 32 countries, most often sport physicians (46%), with therapists, general practitioners, neuropsychologists and other medical practitioners. Analyses were descriptive, with chi-squared tests for associations between profession and familiarity, and between eye tracking experience and perceived benefit.
paper.findings: Eleven percent of respondents had experience working with eye tracking, 66% had heard of it but never used it, and 88% did not use it in practice. Seventy-seven percent used no eye movement assessment tool beyond their own clinical assessment, and 20% did not check for any eye movement deficit; those who did check reported at least one deficit in 29.9% of concussed patients on average. Profession was associated with familiarity (chi-squared p = 0.004), and eye tracking experience was associated with perceived benefit (chi-squared p = 0.015).
paper.limitations: The response rate could not be determined, so non-response and selection bias cannot be ruled out, and self-report may be affected by social desirability. The abstract reports eye tracking use by 12% (consistent with 88% non-use), but only 5% (n = 8) named an eye tracking device or saccadometer as a tool they use to diagnose concussion, so use figures depend on which question is read. The sample was small and mostly from South Africa, Europe and North America, so the authors could not compare regions.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians should note that the survey shows low awareness of eye movement deficits after concussion and a lack of access to eye tracking equipment. Education and hands-on exposure to eye tracking may be needed before clinicians can judge its value. The paper does not show that eye tracking improves diagnosis, so it should not be used to justify changes to concussion protocols.
paper.athleteDev: This survey addresses concussion assessment among clinicians and does not measure athletic performance or training. It cannot inform athlete development.
paper.rtp: The study does not test eye tracking as a return-to-play tool and reports no diagnostic accuracy data. It can show how clinicians currently assess concussion and which tool limitations they report, but it cannot support an eye tracking return-to-play protocol.

records.sourceFile: Beyond the Yard Line - Accommodating Rounded Sports Data in Statistical Models.pdf

paper.citation: Glazer AK, Parast L, Hooten MB. Beyond the Yard Line: Accommodating Rounded Sports Data in Statistical Models. The American Statistician. 2025.
paper.abstract: Recorded American football yardage is a whole number produced by a floor-based rounding of line-of-scrimmage and downed-spot positions, and it can be negative and strongly right-skewed. The authors build parametric models that treat the true yardage as unrounded, derive the discrete probability mass function for the recorded data, and compare rounded-normal and rounded asymmetric Laplace models using 2023 NFL running back data.
paper.tldr: Recorded rushing yards are rounded, can be negative, and are right-skewed, so standard continuous models can mislead. In 2023 NFL running back data, a rounded asymmetric Laplace model fit better than a rounded normal model and changed which players and covariates looked important.
paper.methods: Bayesian models with a discrete likelihood derived from a floor-rounding transformation were fitted by MCMC. A single-player model (Bijan Robinson, 193 carries) and a hierarchical model with a player random intercept (133 running backs, 10,223 carries) were compared using posterior predictive checks and DIC. Covariates included down, yards to go, line of scrimmage, score differential, game seconds remaining, rest, opponent rushing EPA, home-field status and travel distance.
paper.findings: The rounded normal model failed posterior predictive checks for skewness and kurtosis (p of 0.001 or less), while the rounded asymmetric Laplace model did not (p of 0.06 and 0.09), and it had lower DIC in both analyses. In the hierarchical model the authors report 8 of 12 fixed effects with credible intervals not overlapping zero under the asymmetric Laplace model (one, down squared, only nearly so) versus 5 of 12 under the normal model, and C. McCaffrey fell from 2nd to 17th in the player random-intercept ranking.
paper.limitations: The authors assume yardlines are always rounded down, but NFL record-keeping sometimes differs, and some 1-yard-to-go plays (4.7% of 2023 plays are recorded as 1 yard to go) can erase physical gains. Only rushing was modeled, true unrounded yardage was not observed because ball-tracking data were unavailable, and the analysis covers one season with no external validation.
paper.practicalImplications: Analysts who build player-evaluation or yardage models from recorded NFL yardage can use the rounded models described here to avoid treating whole-number, skewed yardage as continuous normal data. Model choice changed some player rankings and covariate conclusions in this sample, so sensitivity checks against a skewed base distribution are worth running.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Applicable to analysis of running back rushing performance data. The paper supports choosing a skewed, discrete model for recorded yards per carry. Its covariate findings (for example, game seconds remaining or yards to go) are model associations from one NFL season and are not coaching prescriptions.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The paper models recorded rushing yardage in healthy professional players and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Calculating acute-chronic workload      ratios using exponentially weighted moving averages provides a more      sensitive indicator of injury likelihood than rolling averages.pdf

paper.citation: Murray NB, Gabbett TJ, Townshend AD, Blanch P. Calculating acute:chronic workload ratios using exponentially weighted moving averages provides a more sensitive indicator of injury likelihood than rolling averages. Br J Sports Med. 2017;51(9):749-754.
paper.abstract: Compared rolling-average and exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) models and their link to non-contact time-loss injury in 59 elite AFL players over two seasons using GPS data. EWMA ACWR values were significantly lower than rolling-average values at moderate, high and very high ranges, and ACWR above 2.0 was associated with higher injury risk under both models, with EWMA explaining more of the injury variance.
paper.tldr: In elite AFL players, the EWMA ACWR gave lower values than rolling averages at moderate to very high ranges and explained more injury variance. Both models linked very high ACWR spikes (above 2.0) to higher injury risk, so the spike signal is the more solid finding.
paper.methods: Two-season cohort of 59 AFL players from one club (92 individual seasons), with 10 Hz GPS workloads for six variables and non-contact time-loss injuries recorded by club medical staff. ACWR was calculated with rolling 7-day and 28-day averages and with EWMA, and binary logistic regression modelled injury against ACWR range.
paper.findings: ACWR above 2.0 was associated with higher injury risk under both models for several variables, for example in-season total distance (rolling average RR 6.52, 95% CI 4.83 to 8.80; EWMA RR 21.28, 95% CI 20.02 to 22.62), each compared with an ACWR of 1.0 to 1.49. The EWMA model gave significantly lower ACWR values than rolling averages at moderate (1.07 vs 1.19), high (1.27 vs 1.64) and very high (1.51 vs 2.29) ranges, and explained more of the variance in injury for total distance (preseason R2 0.87 vs 0.21; in-season 0.78 vs 0.40).
paper.limitations: One club, 59 players and 40 injuries limit generalisation, and the authors note possible type I error from multiple models and small samples above 2.0. The abstract gives a high-speed distance RR range of 5.87 to 13.43, but the Results give 4.66 for rolling-average high-speed distance and 5.87 and 13.43 for player load, so the Results values are used here. The Methods name the 2.0 or above group as reference, while the Results compare against 1.0 to 1.49.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat an ACWR above 2.0 on total distance as a spike to review, since it was the one variable linked to higher non-contact injury risk under both models in both preseason and in-season; under EWMA the same held for moderate-speed distance and player load. Confirm which calculation method a monitoring system uses, because the rolling-average and EWMA values differed for the same day and could place a player in a different risk band.
paper.athleteDev: Use acute:chronic ratios on total distance (and, with EWMA, player load and moderate-speed distance) to flag large workload spikes. The authors also advise building chronic load so acute increases stay moderate, but this study did not test that strategy, and the EWMA method should not replace the rolling-average method as a club standard on the strength of one squad.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tracked non-contact time-loss injuries in squad training and matches and did not assess rehabilitation, readiness or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Can CMJ Neuromuscular Performance Qualities Differentiate Maximal Horizontal Deceleration Ability in Team Sport Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Harper DJ, Cohen DD, Carling C, Kiely J. Can countermovement jump neuromuscular performance qualities differentiate maximal horizontal deceleration ability in team sport athletes? Sports. 2020;8:76.
paper.abstract: Cross-sectional study of 27 male university team-sport athletes who performed a 20 m sprint followed by a maximal horizontal deceleration, measured by radar, and a countermovement jump on force plates. Athletes split at the median on average deceleration (HDEC) or horizontal braking impulse (HBI) differed in several CMJ eccentric and concentric variables, with force variables standing out for HDEC and velocity variables for HBI. Only concentric mean power differed for both measures.
paper.tldr: Concentric force and power from a countermovement jump separated university team-sport athletes with higher from lower horizontal deceleration ability. Average deceleration and braking impulse pointed to different jump profiles, so both should be reported when profiling deceleration.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional design in which 27 male university athletes completed a 20 m sprint and a maximal horizontal deceleration test measured by radar (47 Hz), and five CMJs on dual portable force plates (1000 Hz). Athletes were median-split into high and low HDEC and separately into high and low HBI groups, and CMJ variables were compared with independent-samples t-tests and Cohen's ds with 90% CIs. Test-retest CV was 4.3% for HDEC and 3.7% for HBI.
paper.findings: The high HDEC group had higher concentric peak force (25.87 vs 23.53 N/kg, p=0.02, ds=0.95), concentric mean force (20.07 vs 18.86 N/kg, p=0.03) and concentric mean power (28.72 vs 25.92 W/kg, p=0.04, ds=0.85). Eccentric peak force was higher but not significant (24.66 vs 22.89 N/kg, p=0.07, ds=0.72). For HBI, the high group had higher concentric peak velocity (2.76 vs 2.52 m/s, p=0.01, ds=1.15), concentric peak power (52.39 vs 45.98 W/kg, p=0.01), concentric mean power (28.76 vs 25.67 W/kg, p=0.02) and CMJ height (36.8 vs 29.9 cm, p=0.01), and a faster (more negative) eccentric peak velocity (-1.30 vs -1.10 m/s, p=0.02). High HBI athletes were heavier (85.2 vs 68.1 kg).
paper.limitations: Cross-sectional design, 27 young male university athletes with 13 to 14 per group, and no test of whether training changes deceleration. The Results text gives concentric peak power as -52.39 W/kg, while Table 4 gives 52.39, and the Discussion gives concentric peak velocity as 2.72 m/s and eccentric peak force as 22.69 N/kg, while Tables 3 and 4 give 2.76 and 22.89. The Figure 3 text gives a concentric peak force effect size of 0.52 (Table 3: 0.95), and the group body masses in Table 2 do not average to the 73.0 kg reported for the whole sample; table values are used here. Many comparisons were run without correction, and the authors note the sample is not representative of female athletes or other sports.
paper.practicalImplications: When profiling horizontal deceleration, record both average deceleration and braking impulse, since in this sample they separated athletes on different CMJ variables and braking impulse depends on body mass. Concentric mean power was the one CMJ variable that differed between groups on both measures, so it may be a useful snapshot of neuromuscular capacity for deceleration.
paper.athleteDev: Use the CMJ as a monitoring snapshot alongside sprint-to-deceleration testing, and record body mass, since heavier athletes carry more approach momentum. The paper's suggested training changes, such as accentuated eccentric loading or fast eccentric squats, were not tested here and should be treated as hypotheses.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. Participants were university athletes with no musculoskeletal injury in the previous three months, and the study did not assess injured athletes or readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: Can Player Tracking Devices Monitor Changes in Internal Response During Multidirectional Running .pdf

paper.citation: Oxendale CL, Highton J, Smith G, Twist C. Can player tracking devices monitor changes in internal response during multidirectional running? Res Q Exerc Sport. 2023;94(4):975-981.
paper.abstract: Compared movement, physiological and muscle function responses to linear and multidirectional running in 12 team-sport athletes. Multidirectional running gave more accelerations, more time at high metabolic power, higher summated heart rate and higher bout 8 blood lactate, while linear running gave more high-speed distance. Ratios using time at high metabolic power did not differ significantly between trials, whereas high-speed ratios did, and the authors conclude that time at high metabolic power better reflects the internal response to multidirectional running.
paper.tldr: In 12 team-sport athletes, multidirectional running raised summated heart rate and late blood lactate despite less high-speed distance than linear running. Ratios of time at high metabolic power to internal load did not differ significantly between trials while high-speed ratios did, which the authors read as high metabolic power better reflecting the internal response; this is a small, single-session comparison.
paper.methods: Repeated-measures study with two trials (linear, 3 x 35 m sprints with jogs; and multidirectional, with accelerations, decelerations, sprinting, backward and lateral running) of eight 60 s bouts with 120 s rest, on an outdoor track, in random order. An OptimEye S5 GPS unit (10 Hz) recorded external load; heart rate, VO2 and blood lactate were recorded as internal responses, with isometric knee peak torque before and after each trial. External:internal ratios were compared with paired t-tests and effect sizes.
paper.findings: Multidirectional running produced more accelerations (48.3 vs 7.2) and decelerations (38.8 vs 3.8) than linear running (p<0.001), and more time at high metabolic power (118.4 vs 111.5 s, p=0.046). Summated heart rate (78.1 vs 69.1 AU, p=0.003) and bout 8 blood lactate (10.2 vs 8.2 mmol/L, p=0.002) were higher in the multidirectional trial, while high-speed distance was higher in the linear trial (677.2 vs 416.5 m, p<0.001). Total VO2 did not differ significantly (46.9 vs 44.2 L, p=0.087). Ratios for high-speed running against summated heart rate and total VO2 differed between trials (p<=0.001), while ratios for high metabolic power against these internal measures were similar (p>=0.246). Peak knee extensor and flexor torque fell after both trials (p=0.004 and p=0.003, small effects), with similar falls between trials.
paper.limitations: Twelve athletes, pooled across sexes and sports, with the same participants and data collection as an earlier report by the same group, although these variables were not previously reported. Only one trial per condition was run, running technique was not controlled, the multidirectional trial lasted longer (1428 vs 1382 s), and GPS repeatability for acceleration and deceleration counts is less certain than for distance. The ratio results are non-significant differences, not evidence of equivalence, and no metric was compared against a criterion measure.
paper.practicalImplications: When monitoring multidirectional sessions, do not rely on high-speed distance alone, since it was much lower in the multidirectional trial even though heart rate and blood lactate were higher. Time at high metabolic power can be used alongside high-speed distance, with the caution that this study gives only a small, single-session comparison.
paper.athleteDev: Use time at high metabolic power, together with heart rate or blood lactate where available, to judge the internal demand of multidirectional drills and games, rather than high-speed distance alone. Treat the threshold choice as a practical convention, since the study did not test whether the 20 W/kg cut-off predicts individual responses better than other settings.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It recruited university athletes and did not test injured athletes or return-to-play decisions. The authors suggest the metric might help when moving from linear to multidirectional work after injury, but this was not tested.

records.sourceFile: Causes of Different Force–Velocity Relationships in Sprint Running Depending on Horizontal Loads and Profiling Methods.pdf

paper.citation: Sugisaki N, Tsuchie H, Takai Y, Kobayashi K, Yoshimoto T, Kanehisa H. Causes of Different Force-Velocity Relationships in Sprint Running Depending on Horizontal Loads and Profiling Methods. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025;57(5):1032-1042.
paper.abstract: This study clarified how the horizontal force-velocity relationship in overground sprint running differs with horizontal resistance loads and with profiling methods (multiple-trial and single-trial). Twelve males sprinted unresisted and with five resistance loads while ground reaction forces were recorded on a 50-m force plate system. Force-velocity plots overlapped during acceleration but deviated to lower forces near maximal velocity, the single-trial linear parameters depended on load, and the multiple-trial linear relationship was biased toward lower forces with less negative slopes. Curvilinear models fitted the pooled data better, while the unresisted linear relationship was almost linear.
paper.tldr: Using a 50-m force plate, the sprint force-velocity profile changed with resistance load and with profiling method. The authors recommend the single-trial method with a linear fit to unresisted sprinting over the multiple-trial method for over-ground sprint profiling.
paper.methods: Twelve males each completed six sprints: one unresisted and five resisted at 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 kg, pulled by a motorized loading device, in ascending load order with at least 5 minutes of rest between trials. Horizontal and vertical ground reaction forces were sampled at 1000 Hz, and step-averaged force-velocity profiles were built with single-trial and multiple-trial methods and fitted with linear, Hill's equation and second-order polynomial models.
paper.findings: Force-velocity plots overlapped across loads during acceleration, but horizontal force dropped near maximal velocity. With the single-trial method, F0 rose and the slope became more negative with heavier loads (unresisted F0 7.26 N/kg, 12 kg 8.67 N/kg), while Pmax did not differ significantly. The multiple-trial method gave lower F0 (6.08 N/kg), lower Pmax and a less negative slope (-0.60 vs -0.71 N/kg per m/s) than the unresisted single-trial method, and curvilinear models fitted the pooled data better (adjusted R2 0.986 to 0.987) than a linear fit to the pooled data (0.977) or the unresisted linear profile (0.964).
paper.limitations: This study used 12 men (nine sprinters and three soccer players) and a fixed ascending load order, and the authors could not measure fatigue, so they cannot exclude a fatigue effect on the force drop near maximal velocity. Only step-averaged values were analysed, and intra-step and stance-averaged analyses were not done. The curvilinear models have more parameters, so part of their better fit reflects extra degrees of freedom, and some participants had very high F0 values (up to 12.3 N/kg).
paper.practicalImplications: For over-ground sprint profiling with force plates, follow the authors' recommendation to use the unresisted single-trial method with a linear fit, rather than fitting loaded trials at maximal velocity. Force-velocity values from different profiling methods are not interchangeable, so F0 and slope values should not be compared across studies that used different methods. Loaded sprints should not be assumed to reproduce the profile of unresisted sprints, particularly at very low velocities.
paper.athleteDev: The authors suggest the unresisted single-trial linear profile is the more practical choice for profiling sprint force-velocity, because its fit is close to the curvilinear fits. The paper does not measure performance, and its performance links (v0 and Pmax, not F0) come from earlier studies it cites.
paper.rtp: This study does not address injury or return to sport, and its participants were male sprinters and soccer players. It cannot be used to judge rehabilitation or return-to-play readiness from loaded sprint force data.

records.sourceFile: Changing the criteria applied to acceleration and deceleration efforts changes the types of player actions detected (1).pdf

paper.citation: Ellens S, Carey D, Gastin P, Varley MC. Changing the criteria applied to acceleration and deceleration efforts changes the types of player actions detected. Science and Medicine in Football. 2022.
paper.abstract: Acceleration and deceleration efforts of 22 elite Australian football players across two matches were labeled with the player action at the time, using synchronized video and 10-Hz GNSS data. Linear movement and jumps were most common in high accelerations, and stops and tackles in high decelerations. The authors report that higher commencing speed was linked to longer durations above the deceleration threshold.
paper.tldr: In elite Australian football, high accelerations were mostly linear running and high decelerations mostly stops and contact actions, and the actions captured shift with the minimum duration above threshold. The authors suggest a dwell time of at least 0.5 s if the goal is to count linear accelerations.
paper.methods: Efforts above plus or minus 3 m/s2 were detected from filtered 10-Hz GNSS data for 22 players, and each effort was labeled with one of 15 player actions by manual video coding in Hudl Sportscode. Linear mixed models with player and game random effects tested commencing speed by action and commencing speed against effort duration.
paper.findings: High accelerations were mostly linear movement (about 5 per player per match) and jumps, and high decelerations were mostly stops (about 10 per player per match), being tackled (6) and tackling (4). Commencing speed differed by action only for decelerations, with jumps (+14%, P=.022) and tackles (+17%, P=.003) starting faster than stops, and each 1 m/s higher commencing speed added 0.14 s above the deceleration threshold (95% CI 0.12 to 0.16). Most high accelerations exceeded the threshold for 0.3 s or less (228 of 268 by the reported counts), while about half of decelerations did.
paper.limitations: Two matches from one elite team, a single absolute 3 m/s2 threshold, and device validity taken from manufacturer testing only. Reported numbers do not fully reconcile: 46 efforts per player per match across 22 players and two matches does not match the 1,178 total, the duration counts sum to 1,172, and the Discussion states that most deceleration efforts lasted 0.3 s or less although the counts put about half there. The 0.5 s recommendation for linear movement is read from a histogram, not tested, and only about 30 acceleration efforts lasted 0.5 s or more.
paper.practicalImplications: Choose the minimum duration above threshold to match the actions of interest, because the mix of detected actions changes with it. The authors also recommend training accelerations and decelerations across a range of commencing speeds; this follows from the speed spread observed but was not tested as a training intervention.
paper.athleteDev: If the aim is to count linear accelerations, a longer minimum duration (the authors suggest 0.5 s) helps exclude jumps and other actions. Set the minimum duration to match the action of interest rather than accepting the software default.
paper.rtp: Not applicable: this is match profiling in healthy elite players with no injury or return-to-play outcome. The link between high decelerations and muscle damage that the authors cite comes from other work and was not tested here.

records.sourceFile: Classification of lower body strength qualities - A data-driven approach.pdf

paper.citation: Geneau MC, Gastin PB, Robertson S, James LP. Classification of lower body strength qualities: A data-driven approach. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2025:1-24.
paper.abstract: This systematic review grouped lower-body extensor strength metrics from multi-joint, weight-bearing tests by how much variance they share. The authors propose five domains of lower-body strength: reactive dynamic, unloaded dynamic, loaded dynamic, early isometric and maximal isometric. They call for more empirical work to test these domains before they are used in practice.
paper.tldr: Lower-body strength metrics appear to fall into five groups that measure different things, which may help choose a smaller test battery. Treat the grouping as a proposal: the relationships depend on how each metric is calculated, and no single study has tested the full classification.
paper.methods: Systematic search (September 2024) of Google Scholar, MEDLINE, SportDiscus, Cochrane and CINAHL, English language, no date limit, with reference-list checks. Included studies assessed multi-joint, vertical, dynamic or isometric lower-body tests in athletes or resistance-trained people and compared metrics statistically. Metrics were classified by muscle action, external load and time constraint, then compared within and across categories, with 49% or more shared variance (r of 0.70 or more) treated as similar. No meta-analysis was performed.
paper.findings: Within most task categories, metrics shared more than 50% of variance, except timing and outcome metrics in unloaded ballistic tasks, which shared about 1 to 10%. Drop and rebound jump metrics shared only about 50% of variance with other dynamic and isometric tests, and drop-jump RSI correlated with 1 to 3RM at r = 0.07 to 0.33 in absolute and r = 0.52 to 0.69 in relative values. CMJ height and peak power shared R2 from 0.07 to 0.94 across studies depending on calculation method, and the authors propose five domains while grouping unloaded ballistic timing and outcome metrics into one domain because evidence for separating them was insufficient.
paper.limitations: The authors state that variable methods and populations limit consolidation, the 49% threshold is a simplification, most studies were cross-sectional, and highly correlated metrics can reflect different physiology. The authors say it is unclear where loaded ballistic tasks belong, yet loaded dynamic is listed as a domain, and the five domains need direct testing. The acknowledgements state the work is part of a PhD project partially funded by VALD Performance, while the funding statement reports no financial support.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors recommend a parsimonious test battery, so choosing one test per proposed domain is a reasonable starting point to test. For drop-jump tasks, check that contact time stays under 0.25 s, and confirm how each metric is calculated before comparing values across tools or studies.
paper.athleteDev: The domains can help decide which strength qualities a test battery covers, so that staff do not run several tests that measure the same quality. Because the domains are a proposal, confirm them with each sport's athletes before using them to set training priorities.
paper.rtp: The review does not study injured athletes or return-to-sport criteria, so it cannot set return-to-play thresholds. It can only help choose lower-body strength tests, and the reactive and maximal isometric domains would need checking in injured groups before use in return-to-sport testing.
